desc:
Ecommerce event tracking for shopper actions records what visitors do on your store, from product views to checkout steps. Ecom Swift LLC plans a short list of events with you, builds them in Google Analytics and tests each one.

## What is event tracking, and why does it matter?

Event tracking records a specific action a visitor takes, such as viewing a product, adding it to the cart, using search or starting checkout. In Google Analytics 4, almost everything is an event, so a good setup is really a good list of events with sensible names and details.

Without events, a report tells you that people visited and little more. You cannot see whether they found the product, whether the size filter helped or whether they left at the shipping step. With events, every page becomes a place where you can measure what shoppers actually do.

## How shopper events improve decisions

Events turn vague worries into specific questions. If product views are high and add to cart is low, the product page needs work. If add to cart is healthy but checkout starts are low, the cart page or shipping costs may be scaring people off. If many shoppers use search and then leave, your catalog or search results may not match what they want.

Events also feed everything else. Conversion tracking, funnel reports, audiences and ad optimization all depend on them. A clean event plan means you build once and reuse the data across reports instead of patching each new need.

Custom details add depth. Attaching product type, coupon code or collection name to an event lets you compare groups, such as sales from a discount code against sales without one.

## What a solid event setup includes

- A short event plan listing each event, its trigger and the question it answers.
- The standard ecommerce events: view item, view item list, add to cart, begin checkout and purchase.
- Item details on events, including ID, name, category, price and quantity.
- Site search tracking that records the term shoppers type.
- Filter and sort tracking on collection pages.
- Form events for newsletter sign-ups and contact requests.
- Button clicks for actions that do not load a new page, such as opening a size guide.
- Scroll and video tracking where those behaviors matter to you.
- Consistent naming, in lowercase with underscores, so reports stay readable.
- An event list document that explains each name in plain words.

## How we build and test your events

We begin by asking what you want to learn. A store with a long catalog may care about search and filters. A store with a single hero product may care about video plays and scroll depth. We turn those answers into a short list, because too many events create noise.

Then we build the events in Google Analytics, using Google Tag Manager or your platform's own tools. Where your theme already sends events, we check them, fix mistakes and avoid creating copies. We also decide which details travel with each event, so reports can later be split by product, category or coupon.

Every event is tested in debug mode. We click through the store as a shopper and watch each event appear with the right name and details. Basic covers the core ecommerce events. Standard adds search, filters, forms and button clicks. Premium adds custom details, scroll and video tracking, an Explorations report built in Analytics, and a handover call.

## Do and avoid

**Do:**
- Start with the questions you need answered, then choose events.
- Use clear names that a colleague can understand.
- Send item details with every ecommerce event.
- Test events again after any theme update.
- Keep the event list document up to date.

**Avoid:**
- Tracking every click on the page.
- Creating two events for the same action.
- Putting personal data such as email addresses into event details.
- Renaming events later without noting the date.
- Assuming a theme tracks everything it appears to.

## Who event tracking is for

It suits stores that have Analytics installed but only see visits and sessions. It fits owners about to run a conversion project who need to know where shoppers stall, and it helps teams that have inherited a property full of unclear events and want order restored. A store planning a theme change should also plan events first, so tracking survives the move.

Events appear in debug view straight away, while standard reports can take a day to fill in.

## What we need from you

Tell us what you want to learn about shoppers, and give us access to your store, your analytics property and your tag manager if you have one. Access can be collaborator, staff or editor roles. If your theme was customized, tell us who built it. We never need your passwords, and you keep ownership of every account and container.
